newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Ringgit seen less volatile after bank meeting.
newsitem.headline: Ringgit seen less volatile after bank meeting.

text.p: Recent gyrations in the Malaysian ringgit are expected to diminish after last week's meeting between bankers and the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, economists said on Wednesday.
Top officials of Bank Negara on Friday met chief executives of some local and locally-incorporated foreign banks over foreign exchange activities, said banking sources.

Although there was no official statement about what was discussed at the meeting, the market believed that the central bank was recruiting help from banks in the event that the ringgit comes under another speculative attack.
Officials at Bank Negara declined to comment on the meeting.
The Malaysian currency last month came under attack from speculators in the wake of a financial crisis in Thailand. Bank Negara intervened aggressively to stem the ringgit's slide.

"Such a move to seek reinforcement is deemed necessary after the central bank's foreign reserves at end-May fell 1.4 billion ringgit ($558 million) to 69.7 billion ringgit compared to a fortnight earlier, reflecting its intervention efforts to support the ringgit during the baht fiasco," said research house MMS International in a report.
Dealers and economists said the central bank move was not surprising given the uncertainty in Thailand and possibility of a fresh speculative attack on the ringgit.

Some said Bank Negara could also have told the banks, believed to be those with the largest foreign exchange operations and highest exposure to swaps, that if they continue to deal with speculators, the central bank would not help them at times when they need ringgit.
This will indirectly restrict offshore players' access to the local forwards market, thus limiting further advance in forward rates.

"Bank Negara wants to make sure there's not so much hot money flowing around after what happened in Thailand. It's just a pre-emptive check," said Jimmy Koh, an economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
But Andrew Fung, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said getting co-operation from banks would not be easy.
"Banks have positions and they have to go with customers flow. They cannot be going the opposite way," he said. "But I don't think we will see a repeat of what happened in May."
Dealers and economists said in the immediate term, they expected the ringgit to continue tracking a tight range of 2.5050-2.5200 against the dollar.

Corporate dollar sales out of Kuala Lumpur and fears of intervention by Bank Negara had capped the dollar's topside at 2.5200 in recent weeks. The central bank was last heard checking rates at the 2.5190/5200 level.
At 0330 GMT, the ringgit was quoted at 2.5095/05 a dollar.
For the longer term, international confidence in the Malaysian economy and high local interest rates would favour the ringgit, economists said.
Interbank rates have stayed firm due to a liquidity squeeze caused by the central bank intervention last month.

Some dealers said rates were being kept high by Bank Negara to ward off speculators as it will be expensive to maintain short ringgit positions. But the central bank has said that the rise in interest rates was a temporary phenomenon.
"I'm looking at ringgit hitting 2.47 (per dollar) this year," said Fung of Standard Chartered Bank.
($1=2.51 ringgit)
